question: What is the main job of hormones in our bodies?

options.A: Generate fast electrical impulses for muscle movement
options.B: Fight off bacterial infections in the bloodstream
options.C: Digest food particles inside the stomach lumen
options.D: Act as chemical messengers to regulate body functions

explanation: Think of hormones as the body's postal service! They are chemical messengers sent out by glands to travel through the blood and help manage how different organs work. You've got this! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h1)

question: How does the endocrine system's signaling mainly differ from the nervous system?

options.A: Nervous signaling relies entirely on blood transport systems
options.B: Endocrine signaling uses fast electrical impulses directly to tissues
options.C: Nervous signaling controls long-term growth instead of rapid reflexes
options.D: Endocrine signaling is slower and provides longer-lasting control

explanation: While nerves give quick, snap reactions (like pulling your hand from fire), hormones take a bit longer to travel through the blood, but their effects stick around much longer. Great to know for clinical practice! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h1)

question: Which substance serves as the main chemical building block for steroid hormones?
explanation: Steroid hormones are made straight from cholesterol! Even though people often talk about cholesterol in a bad nutritional light, our bodies actually need it to build vital hormones. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h2)

question: Why is it helpful for nurses to know a hormone's chemical structure?

options.A: It shows whether the hormone is made of white blood cells
options.B: It predicts how they travel in blood and interact with target cells
options.C: It dictates the exact caloric value of the hormone in the diet
options.D: It determines the exact time of day the gland will secrete them

explanation: Knowing whether a hormone is water-soluble or fat-soluble helps us understand how it moves through the blood and finds its target. Clinical pharmacology becomes much easier when you master this basics! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h2)

question: Which amino acid is the starting point for making catecholamines and thyroid hormones?
explanation: Tyrosine is the key building block amino acid used to manufacture important hormones like adrenaline and your thyroid hormones. One step at a time, you're learning it! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h3)

question: What makes thyroid hormones act a bit differently than other amino acid-derived hormones?

options.A: They are large proteins made of hundreds of linked amino acids
options.B: They only function within the nervous system as fast neurotransmitters
options.C: They cannot travel in the bloodstream without dissolving in red blood cells
options.D: They are fat-soluble and enter cells to bind intracellular receptors

explanation: Even though they start from an amino acid, thyroid hormones behave like fat-loving steroids—they slip right inside the cell to do their work. Tricky, but you'll never forget it now! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h3)

question: How do peptide and protein hormones typically travel through the bloodstream?

options.A: They require specialized carrier proteins to move through blood
options.B: They precipitate out of solution if not bound to electrolytes
options.C: They are water-soluble and dissolve freely in blood plasma
options.D: They are fat-soluble and travel inside red blood cells

explanation: Because protein and peptide hormones love water, they dissolve easily right into the watery plasma of your blood and swim along freely without needing a special ride. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h4)

question: Where do water-soluble peptide hormones usually find their target cell receptors?

options.A: On the outer surface of the target cell membrane
options.B: Attached to the outer wall of blood capillaries
options.C: Deep inside the nucleus of the target cell
options.D: Floating freely within the cytoplasm of the cell

explanation: Since water-soluble hormones can't cross the fatty cell membrane barrier, they have to knock on the front door by binding to receptors on the outside surface of the cell. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h4)

question: Which of these is a well-known example of a steroid hormone?
explanation: Cortisol is our classic stress steroid hormone, made by the adrenal cortex straight from cholesterol. You'll hear about cortisol constantly in medical-surgical nursing! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h5)

question: If a newly discovered hormone passes right through cell membranes without needing a surface receptor, what is it likely made of?
explanation: Fat likes fat! Because steroid hormones are lipid-soluble, they slide smoothly across the fatty cell membrane to reach receptors inside. Brilliant deduction! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h5)

question: Why do fat-soluble hormones need carrier proteins to travel in the blood?

options.A: Carrier proteins are needed to digest the hormone
options.B: They do not mix well with the watery plasma
options.C: They are too heavy to float without assistance
options.D: They would instantly destroy red blood cells if free

explanation: Oil and water don't mix! Since fat-soluble hormones don't dissolve in watery blood plasma, they need special carrier proteins to give them a ride through the circulatory system. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h6)

question: Which portion of a fat-soluble hormone in the blood is actually active and able to affect cells?

options.A: The large fraction securely attached to liver carrier proteins
options.B: The small fraction that remains unbound or free in the blood
options.C: The portion that gets trapped inside blood vessel walls
options.D: The total amount secreted by the endocrine gland combined

explanation: Only the free, unattached hormones can slip out of the blood vessels to do their job. The rest stay safely hitched to their carrier proteins like passengers on a bus! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h6)

question: What system do water-soluble hormones use to pass along messages inside a cell?
explanation: Since water-soluble hormones can't enter the cell themselves, they drop their message off at the surface, triggering a 'second messenger' inside the cell to carry out the orders. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h7)

question: Once a fat-soluble hormone gets inside a target cell, what is its main task?

options.B: Release calcium stores from the cell membrane
options.C: Regulate gene expression and protein synthesis
options.D: Block electrical impulses from the nervous system

explanation: Fat-soluble hormones go straight to the control center (the nucleus) to interact with DNA, turning specific genes on or off to make new proteins. You're crushing these physiology concepts! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h7)
